routes.SELL: Has scrap value. A kabadiwala or authorised buyer pays for this.
routes.BIN_DRY: Dry waste bin (blue). No value, but recyclable stream.
routes.SPECIAL: Must NOT go in either bin. Regulated or hazardous route only.

_meta.WARNING: All value figures and all facility details are UNVERIFIED drafts. Every entry with a non-empty verify array must be confirmed by phone before this ships. Do not present unverified prices to judges as fact.

legal_refs.SWM2016: Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016 - mandates wet/dry/domestic-hazardous segregation at source
legal_refs.EWASTE2022: E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022 - EPR, authorised dismantlers registered with CPCB
legal_refs.CND2016: Construction and Demolition Waste Management Rules, 2016
legal_refs.RUCO: FSSAI Repurpose Used Cooking Oil initiative

_meta.content_note: why_not_bin / steps / learn are teaching content, written to be specific to the item. learn is always a YouTube SEARCH url, never a video id - a search cannot rot or point at the wrong thing.

categories.name: Newspaper / raddi
categories.destination: Any local kabadiwala. Highest-value household stream, already widely sold.
categories.why_not_bin: Paper tipped in with wet waste turns to pulp within hours and stops being sellable. It is the easiest money in the house to lose.
steps: Keep it dry. Damp raddi is refused or paid at half rate.
Stack flat and tie with string, not tape - tape has to be picked off.
Weigh it yourself first. Spring scales under-read in the buyer's favour.
Ask the rate per kilo before you hand it over, not after.

categories.name: Cardboard / corrugated boxes
categories.destination: Local kabadiwala. Flatten first - they pay by weight but refuse bulky loose boxes.

reuse.note: Intact boxes are worth more to small e-commerce sellers than to a scrap dealer.

categories.why_not_bin: Loose boxes fill the bin in minutes and the collector often refuses them. Flattened, the same boxes are a paid stream.
steps: Strip packing tape and plastic couriers labels off.
Flatten every box - buyers pay by weight but refuse bulky loose cartons.
Keep it dry; wet corrugate loses most of its value.
An intact sturdy box is worth more resold to a small online seller than as scrap.

categories.name: PET plastic bottles
categories.destination: Kabadiwala. Clear PET pays more than coloured. Caps are a different polymer.
categories.why_not_bin: A capped bottle is mostly trapped air. It fills the bag, and if it still has liquid in it, it wets everything sellable around it.
steps: Empty it completely and give it a rinse.
Take the cap off - it is a different polymer and is sold separately.
Crush it flat so it stops taking up space.
Keep clear PET away from coloured. Clear fetches a noticeably better rate.

categories.name: Mixed / soft plastic, wrappers
categories.destination: Dry bin. Multilayer packaging has effectively no scrap market - this is the honest answer and most apps avoid giving it.
categories.why_not_bin: There is no buyer for multilayer film anywhere in the chain. Worse, dropping it into the recycling sack contaminates the plastic around it that someone was going to be paid for.
steps: Do not put it in the recycling sack. It devalues the whole bag.
Shake out crumbs and food so it does not rot the dry waste.
Dry bin is the honest answer. Nobody downstream wants this.
The only real reduction here is buying fewer, larger packs.

categories.name: Iron / steel scrap
categories.destination: Kabadiwala or scrap metal dealer.
categories.why_not_bin: Steel is endlessly recyclable and has real cash value. In a bin it goes to landfill and someone mines fresh ore instead.
steps: Empty out any plastic or rubber handles - buyers deduct for them.
Keep steel separate from aluminium. Mixed metal is paid at the lower rate.
A magnet sticks to steel and iron. That is your free sorting test.

categories.name: Aluminium
categories.destination: Scrap metal dealer. High value - do not let this go in a bin.
categories.why_not_bin: Recycling aluminium uses a fraction of the energy of smelting it new, and it is one of the highest-paying things in your kitchen. Binned, both are wasted.
steps: Magnet test: a magnet does NOT stick to aluminium but does stick to steel. This one check stops you being paid the steel rate for aluminium.
Rinse off food residue.
Crush cans to save space; foil should be balled up tight, not left loose.

categories.name: Copper wire / fittings
categories.destination: Scrap metal dealer. The single highest-value household stream.
categories.why_not_bin: Copper is the single highest-value thing most households throw out. It is also why cable is burned in the open, which is the dirty way to recover it.
steps: Never burn insulation off. It releases dioxins and buyers pay less for fire-damaged copper anyway.
Strip insulation with a knife if you can - bright bare copper pays far more than insulated wire.
Keep copper apart from brass. They look similar and are priced differently.

categories.name: Glass bottles / jars
categories.hazard: Broken glass injures waste pickers. Wrap shards in newspaper and label.
categories.destination: Kabadiwala, though many refuse low-value glass. Dry bin otherwise.

reuse.note: Intact jars are reused directly in most Delhi kitchens - the highest-value route is your own shelf.

categories.why_not_bin: Loose broken glass in a bag is a direct injury risk to the person who opens it by hand - and that is how most of Delhi's waste is sorted.
steps: Rinse out residue so it does not attract pests.
If it is broken, wrap the pieces in thick newspaper and write GLASS on it.
Intact jars are worth more on your own kitchen shelf than at the scrap rate.

categories.name: Lithium battery / power bank / laptop battery
categories.hazard: FIRE RISK. Punctured or crushed lithium cells ignite. Cells in mixed waste are a documented cause of collection-vehicle and landfill fires. Never bin, never sell to an unauthorised dealer who will cut it open.
categories.destination: CPCB-registered battery recycler or manufacturer take-back. Needs a verified Delhi facility.
categories.why_not_bin: A crushed lithium cell ignites. In a collection vehicle that means a fire with a person standing next to it, and landfill fires at Ghazipur and Bhalswa have started this way.
steps: Tape over both terminals with insulating tape. A loose cell shorting against metal in a bag is the single most common way these catch fire.
Never puncture, crush or try to open it.
If it is swollen or hot, keep it away from anything flammable and do not carry it in a pocket or bag against other metal.
Store it somewhere cool and dry until you can reach a registered recycler.

categories.name: Lead-acid battery (inverter / car)
categories.hazard: Lead and sulphuric acid. Informal breaking is a major lead-poisoning source. Has real resale value, which is exactly why it ends up in unsafe hands.
categories.destination: Dealer take-back on replacement, or registered recycler. Note: the buyer paying most is often the least safe - worth saying so in the UI.
categories.why_not_bin: These have enough resale value that they reliably get bought - the problem is who buys them. Informal breaking spills sulphuric acid and is a serious source of lead poisoning in children nearby.
steps: Keep it upright. A tipped battery leaks acid.
Exchange it at the dealer when buying the replacement - that is the normal and safest route, and you still get the trade-in value.
Be wary of the buyer offering the most cash. That is often the one breaking it open in the open air.

categories.name: CFL bulb / fluorescent tube light
categories.hazard: Contains mercury vapour. Breaking releases it indoors. This is the item almost every household disposes of wrongly.
categories.destination: Authorised e-waste collection point. CONFIRM whether CFL and fluorescent lamps fall under the 2022 schedule before citing the rule on camera.
categories.why_not_bin: Each tube holds a small amount of mercury vapour. Snapped in a bag it is released right where someone is sorting by hand.
steps: Do not snap it to fit the bin. That is the moment the mercury is released.
Slide it back into the old carton, or wrap it in thick paper and label it.
If one does break, open the windows, leave the room for 15 minutes, and sweep with stiff card - never a vacuum, which sprays the vapour around.

categories.name: LED bulb
categories.hazard: No mercury, but contains electronics. Lower urgency than CFL - worth distinguishing, since telling users LED and CFL are identical loses trust.
categories.destination: Authorised e-waste collection point.
categories.why_not_bin: No mercury, but the driver circuit inside is electronics, and electronics in landfill leach metals into groundwater.
steps: No special handling - it is not a mercury risk like CFL.
Keep it with your other small e-waste rather than making a separate trip.

categories.name: Old mobile phone / tablet
categories.hazard: Contains a lithium cell. Wipe data before handing over - this belongs in the UI copy.
categories.destination: Authorised e-waste recycler, or brand take-back / buyback. Seelampur is the large informal e-waste hub in Delhi - name it honestly in the writeup rather than pretending the informal route does not exist.

reuse.note: A working phone is worth far more resold or donated than recycled. Check function before routing.

categories.why_not_bin: A phone holds recoverable gold, silver and copper, plus a lithium cell. It also holds your accounts, photos and bank apps.
steps: Sign out of your accounts FIRST, then factory reset. A reset alone can leave you still signed in on some devices.
Remove the SIM and the memory card. People forget the memory card.
If it still switches on, resale or donation returns far more than recycling.
If the back is swollen, treat it as a damaged lithium cell, not a phone.

categories.name: Mixed e-waste (chargers, cables, remotes, keyboards)
categories.hazard: Mixed metals and plastics. Informal burning to recover copper releases dioxins.
categories.destination: Authorised e-waste recycler.
categories.why_not_bin: Chargers and cables are mostly copper in plastic. The informal way to get that copper out is to burn the plastic off, which is one of the dirtiest things done to Delhi's air.
steps: Collect it up rather than binning items one at a time - a handful is worth a trip.
Keep any item with a battery in it separate from plain cables.
Hand it to an authorised recycler, not to anyone who will burn it for the copper.

categories.name: Expired / unused medicine
categories.hazard: Antibiotics reaching landfill and water contribute to antimicrobial resistance. Flushing is worse, not better.
categories.destination: Hospital medicine drop-box. Many Delhi hospitals keep collection boxes and accept household expired medicine, which then enters their bio-medical waste stream. Note this is a voluntary take-back, not a mandated household route - Bio-Medical Waste Rules bind the facility, not you. VERIFY which hospital near the demo location has a live box.
categories.incentive_lever: SAFETY_ONLY - there is no rupee value here, so the UI must carry this entry on the AMR and child-poisoning framing alone. Do not show an empty price field.
categories.why_not_bin: Antibiotics reaching landfill and groundwater drive drug resistance. Flushing them is worse, not better - it puts them straight into water. Loose tablets in a bin are also a poisoning risk to children and animals.
steps: Do not flush, and do not tip loose tablets into the bin.
Leave them in the original blister and box so the hospital can identify them.
Scratch out your name and the patient details on the label first.
Take them to a hospital collection box, where they enter the bio-medical waste stream and are incinerated properly.

categories.name: Pooja flowers / temple floral waste
categories.hazard: Routinely immersed in the Yamuna. The flowers are benign; the thread, plastic wrap and foil in a garland are not.
categories.destination: Wet bin, or compost. Strip the plastic thread and foil first - the step nobody mentions.

reuse.note: Compost directly, or route to a floral-waste upcycler. Real volume diversion, not craft reuse.

categories.why_not_bin: Flowers themselves rot down harmlessly. What does the damage is everything tied into the garland - plastic thread, foil, pins - which goes into the Yamuna with it and never leaves.
steps: Pull the garland apart and strip out the plastic thread, foil and any pins. This is the step almost everyone skips, and it is the one that matters.
Do not immerse in the Yamuna or any drain. It is prohibited and it is what chokes the river.
Petals go in the green wet bin, or straight into a compost bin or pot.
If you compost at home, mix flowers with dry leaves or newspaper - flowers alone turn into a wet, smelling mat.

categories.name: Used cooking oil
categories.hazard: Down the drain it blocks sewers and reaches the Yamuna. Re-fried it is a health hazard.
categories.destination: FSSAI RUCO collection converts it to biodiesel. VERIFY which Delhi aggregators collect from households rather than only restaurants - this may be bulk-only, which is worth saying plainly.
categories.why_not_bin: Poured down the drain it congeals and is a major cause of sewer blockage, and what gets through reaches the Yamuna. Re-fried, it is a genuine health hazard.
steps: Let it cool completely first.
Strain out the food bits through a cloth or sieve.
Store it in a sealed plastic bottle - never pour it down the sink or drain.
Do not reuse it for frying repeatedly; repeatedly heated oil is the actual risk.

categories.name: Old clothes / textiles
categories.destination: Rarely bought by weight. Traditional route is bartan-badlo barter, or NGO donation.

reuse.note: Wearable clothing should be donated or bartered, never binned. Unwearable cotton becomes industrial rags - a real market.

categories.why_not_bin: Textiles are one of the fastest-growing landfill streams, and wearable clothing being binned while someone nearby needs it is the plainest kind of waste there is.
steps: Wash it before donating. Unwashed donations are usually thrown away.
Split wearable from unwearable - they go to completely different places.
Unwearable cotton still has a market as industrial cleaning rags.
Pair and tie shoes together so they do not get separated in sorting.

categories.name: Furniture / mattress
categories.hazard: Bulky waste. MCD does not collect this in normal door-to-door rounds - the reason these end up on roadsides.
categories.destination: Second-hand dealer, NGO, or MCD bulky-waste arrangement. VERIFY whether your zone runs a bulky-waste pickup.

reuse.note: Repair and resale dominate recycling here by a wide margin.

categories.why_not_bin: Bulky items are excluded from normal door-to-door collection, which is exactly why mattresses and sofas end up abandoned on Delhi roadsides.
steps: Do not leave it out on the street - it will sit there for weeks.
If it is repairable, a second-hand dealer or carpenter will take it.
Mattresses are the hardest item here; check for a bulky-waste pickup before assuming anyone will collect it.

categories.name: Construction debris / malba
categories.hazard: A major Delhi PM10 source, both from the dust and from illegal roadside dumping.
categories.destination: MCD C and D waste processing facility. Delhi operates several plants. VERIFY current site list and whether household quantities are accepted.
categories.why_not_bin: Roadside malba is a significant share of Delhi's PM10 - it is ground to dust by traffic and goes straight into the air you breathe.
steps: Keep it damp and covered while it is stored. Dry malba becomes airborne dust.
Never tip it on a roadside or into a drain.
Bag it rather than loose-piling it so it can actually be collected.

categories.name: Sanitary waste / diapers
categories.hazard: Domestic hazardous under SWM2016. Handling it unwrapped is a direct health risk to waste pickers - the strongest human argument in the table.
categories.destination: Wrap and mark separately as domestic hazardous, per SWM2016. VERIFY how MCD handles the marked stream in your zone.
categories.why_not_bin: Delhi's waste is still largely sorted by hand. Unwrapped sanitary waste in a mixed bag is a direct health risk to the person doing that sorting.
steps: Wrap it in paper - not in another plastic bag, which makes it invisible to the person handling it.
Mark the wrap, even just an X. SWM Rules class this as domestic hazardous, and the marking is what warns the handler.
Keep it out of both the wet and the dry bag.

categories.name: Kitchen / food waste
categories.destination: Green bin. Roughly half of Delhi household waste by weight, and the stream whose mis-sorting ruins every other stream.

reuse.note: Home composting is the highest route. A simple terrace or bokashi bin works in a Delhi flat.

categories.why_not_bin: This is roughly half your waste by weight, and it is the stream that ruins the others - once it is mixed in, the paper, card and plastic around it stop being sellable.
steps: Keep it strictly in the green bin. Mixed in, it devalues everything else.
Drain liquids before binning - weight is what makes collection expensive.
Home composting works in a flat: layer wet kitchen scraps with dry leaves, paper or cocopeat, roughly half and half.
If your compost smells, it needs more dry material and more air, not less waste.

categories.name: Clay pot / crockery / ceramic
categories.hazard: Broken ceramic has sharp edges and is sorted by hand. It also never breaks down - fired clay is inert for good.
categories.why_not_bin: Terracotta and ceramic are inert. They will not rot, will not burn, and nobody buys them, so they just sit. The real harm is the sharp edges: a shattered handi loose in a bag cuts the person who opens it.
steps: An intact pot is worth far more as a planter or a water pot than as waste.
If it is broken, wrap the pieces in thick newspaper and mark it SHARP.
Unglazed terracotta can be crushed and mixed into soil or a potted plant.
Glazed crockery cannot be recycled with glass - the glaze melts differently and contaminates the batch.
categories.destination: Dry bin, wrapped if broken. Large quantities of rubble-like ceramic go with construction debris instead.

reuse.note: An intact matka or handi is a planter, a water cooler or a seed starter. Reuse comfortably beats disposal here.
